title: PowerShell
summary: PowerShell is a scripting language and functional command-line shell built on .NET, used throughout enterprise networks to automate updates, software management, and security tasks at both the server and client level. Every cmdlet follows a strict Verb-Noun naming pattern, everything a cmdlet returns is an object with inspectable properties and methods, and cmdlets chain together through the pipeline (|). Cyber operators lean on this constantly — for enumeration, automation, and remote administration over WinRM.

commands.description: Displays the PowerShell host's version — the quickest way to check whether you're in Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7.x.
Switches the current session into PowerShell 7.x (Core) from Windows PowerShell 5.1. Both versions are installed side by side on modern Windows.
Closes the current PowerShell session and returns to whatever session launched it — the way back from pwsh to 5.1.
Displays help for a cmdlet. -Online opens the Microsoft docs page in a browser; -Full or -Detailed adds parameter descriptions and examples.
Displays an about_ conceptual topic explaining PowerShell's help syntax notation: [-Name] means optional/positional, <type> means a required value.
Lists the cmdlets, functions, and aliases available in the current session. Can be filtered with -Type, -Module, or -Noun.
Shows which cmdlet an alias actually maps to — dir resolves to Get-ChildItem.
Lists every property and method available on the object(s) a cmdlet returns, along with the object's TypeName.
Projects only the named properties from each object in the pipeline, dropping everything else.
Filters piped objects using a script block; $_ represents the current object flowing through the pipeline.
The shorthand Where-Object syntax — -Property -Operator Value — returns the exact same result as the script-block form.
Launches a process, using the .NET Process.Start() method under the hood.
Terminates a running process by name, using the .NET Process.Kill() method under the hood.
Controls how returned objects are displayed — as a compact table (ft) or a one-property-per-line list (fl).
Creates a new file (or -Type Directory for a folder) at the given path.
Deletes an item. -Verbose confirms what happened; -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue hides errors if the item doesn't exist.
Shows the script execution policy for every scope (Machine, User, Process, etc). The default is Restricted.
Changes the script execution policy for a given scope — required before most .ps1 scripts will run.
Queries a CIM class for management data — the modern, faster replacement for the deprecated Get-WmiObject.
Creates the current user's PowerShell profile script, since profiles don't exist by default.
Enables PowerShell Remoting on a client OS. The flag is required when a Public network profile is active, and adds a firewall rule limited to the local subnet.
Runs a script block on a remote computer over WinRM and returns the results — a one-to-one temporary remoting session.
Adds a host to the client's TrustedHosts list, required for WinRM to use NTLM auth outside an Active Directory domain.

terms.description: A native PowerShell command using strict Verb-Noun naming, e.g. Get-Process — nouns are always singular (Get-Process, never Get-Processes).
Passes the output object(s) of one cmdlet as input to the next cmdlet using the | operator, letting commands be chained together.
Represents the current object flowing through the pipeline inside a script block, e.g. {$_.Status -eq "Stopped"}. Always the same type as the object from the previous command.
Everything a PowerShell cmdlet returns is an object with properties (data) and methods (actions) — Get-Member reveals both, plus the object's TypeName.
The protocol PowerShell Remoting uses instead of the older DCOM, built on WS-Management; needs only one firewall port and encrypts traffic with a per-session AES-256 key.
The SOAP-based device-management protocol that WinRM implements, letting PowerShell Remoting simplify network configuration to a single open port.
A vendor-neutral object model for describing management data (hardware, OS, services); WMI classes are built directly on top of CIM classes.
Microsoft's implementation of CIM, used to query and manage Windows subsystems like the BIOS, disks, and processes; Get-CimInstance is its modern successor cmdlet.
Controls whether, and which, PowerShell scripts (.ps1 files) are allowed to run on a system; defaults to Restricted, which blocks nearly everything.
A .ps1 script (not created by default) that runs automatically whenever a matching PowerShell session starts, used to persist aliases, functions, and settings.
A variable PowerShell creates and maintains on its own, e.g. $_, $?, $PSVersionTable, $PROFILE, $HOME, and $ERROR — never assigned by the user.
A short alternate name that maps to a cmdlet, e.g. dir -> Get-ChildItem; aliases you create yourself are lost when the session closes unless saved in a profile.
A client-side list of hosts that PowerShell Remoting will trust for NTLM authentication outside an Active Directory domain, where Kerberos isn't available.
A recorded log of everything typed and returned in a PowerShell session, started with Start-Transcript and ended with Stop-Transcript. Doesn't work inside the ISE.
The older Windows remote-object technology that PowerShell Remoting (via WinRM) was built to replace, requiring more firewall ports and offering weaker encryption.

facts: PowerShell cmdlets follow a strict Verb-Noun naming pattern with a singular noun, e.g. Get-Process, never Get-Processes.
Parameters begin with a dash (-Name) unless they are positional; Get-Service -Name bits and Get-Service bits are functionally identical.
PowerShell 1.0 through 5.1 run on the .NET Framework and are Windows-only; PowerShell Core (pwsh) runs on .NET Core and is cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux).
Windows 10 ships with PowerShell 5.1 by default. Typing pwsh switches into PowerShell 7.x side by side; exit returns to the previous session's version.
Everything a PowerShell cmdlet returns is an object — Get-Member reveals its TypeName plus every property and method available on it.
$_ inside a Where-Object script block always refers to the current object flowing through the pipeline, and is always the same type as the object from the previous command.
Get-Help searches both a cmdlet's own help page and its related about_ conceptual topic at the same time; individual about_ topics can also be searched directly, e.g. Get-Help about_command_syntax.
The default PowerShell script Execution Policy is Restricted, which blocks all scripts not created in the local intranet zone or a workgroup.
PowerShell Remoting (available since PowerShell v2) uses WinRM/WS-Management instead of DCOM, needing only one open firewall port, with traffic encrypted by a per-session AES-256 key.

WinRM defaults to Kerberos authentication on port 5985 (HTTP) or 5986 (HTTPS, requires a certificate). Outside an Active Directory domain, a host must be added to TrustedHosts, or HTTPS must be used instead.
Connecting to a remote session by IP address instead of hostname prevents Kerberos from being used — NTLM authentication is used instead, which requires the target to be listed in TrustedHosts.
PowerShell profiles are plain .ps1 scripts and are not created by default; custom aliases and variables set interactively are lost when the session closes unless they're saved to a profile.

Setting WSMan TrustedHosts to "*" trusts every possible host and overrides one of the strongest built-in protections against spoofed connections and credential theft — acceptable for throwaway testing only, never production.
CIM classes are the vendor-neutral parent model that Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) classes are built on; Get-CimInstance is the modern, faster replacement for the deprecated Get-WmiObject.

Enabling PowerShell Remoting on a client OS with an active Public network profile requires the -SkipNetworkProfileCheck flag on Enable-PSRemoting, which adds a firewall rule limited to hosts on the local subnet.

questions.questionHtml: Which naming convention do all PowerShell cmdlets follow?

options.html: Verb-Noun, with the noun always singular (e.g. Get-Process)
Noun-Verb, with the noun always plural (e.g. Process-Get)
camelCase function names with no hyphen
snake_case command names

questions.explanationHtml: PowerShell cmdlets always use Verb-Noun syntax, and the noun is always singular — Get-Process, never Get-Processes.

questions.questionHtml: You write a PowerShell script against one PowerShell version, then run it against a target running a different version. What should you expect?

options.html: Nothing — scripts are always fully version-independent
A high likelihood of the script failing or producing errors
The script automatically upgrades itself to match the target
PowerShell refuses to load any cross-version script file

questions.explanationHtml: Because functionality and even syntax can differ between versions, a script written for one PowerShell version has a high likelihood of failing or erroring when run against a different version. Always be mindful of the version in use.

questions.questionHtml: Which command switches the current console session from Windows PowerShell 5.1 into PowerShell 7.x?

options.html: switch-ps
pwsh
powershell -v7
Update-PowerShell

questions.explanationHtml: Typing pwsh at the prompt drops you into PowerShell 7.x, since both versions are installed side by side on modern Windows.

questions.questionHtml: After typing pwsh to move from PowerShell 5.1 into 7.3, how do you return to the previous 5.1 session?

options.html: exit
pwsh -exit
Stop-Session
Close-PSSession

questions.explanationHtml: exit closes the current session and drops you back into whichever session launched it — from 7.3 back to 5.1.

questions.questionHtml: Which two statements about PowerShell parameters are correct? (Choose two.)

options.html: Parameters always begin with a dash unless they are positional
PowerShell uses spaces as parameter delimiters
Every parameter must always include a leading dash, with no exceptions
A parameter value containing spaces can never be passed, even in quotes

questions.explanationHtml: Parameters begin with a dash unless they're positional (no dash required), and PowerShell separates parameters with spaces. A value containing spaces just needs to be wrapped in quotes, e.g. Get-Content -Path "C:\Test Files\content.txt".

questions.questionHtml: Get-Service -Name bits is functionally identical to which other command?

options.html: Get-Service Name bits
Get-Service bits
Get-Service -bits
Find-Service bits

questions.explanationHtml: -Name is a positional parameter, so the dash-and-name can be dropped entirely: Get-Service bits means the same thing.

questions.questionHtml: What does running Get-Process | Get-Member show you?

options.html: Only the running process names
The object's TypeName plus every property and method available on it
Live, continuously-updating memory usage
Whether each process binary is digitally signed

questions.explanationHtml: Get-Member returns the TypeName of the piped object (e.g. System.Diagnostics.Process) along with every property and method it exposes.

questions.questionHtml: In Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Stopped"}, what does $_ represent?

options.html: Every service on the system, regardless of status
The current object flowing through the pipeline from the previous command
A variable the user must manually declare beforehand
The literal text "Status"

questions.explanationHtml: $_ is the pipelined variable — it represents whichever object is currently passing through the pipeline, and is always the same type as the object produced by the previous command.

questions.questionHtml: How do the results of Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Stopped"} and Get-Service | where Status -eq "Stopped" compare?

options.html: They return the exact same result — one is just shorthand for the other
Only the script-block form is valid PowerShell syntax
The shorthand form requires piping through Format-Table first to work
"where" is not a recognized alias for Where-Object

questions.explanationHtml: Both are Where-Object — the second just uses the shorthand -Property -Operator Value form and the where alias instead of the full script-block syntax. The results are identical.

questions.questionHtml: What is the default PowerShell script Execution Policy on a fresh Windows installation?

options.html: Unrestricted
Bypass
Restricted
AllSigned

questions.explanationHtml: The default policy is Restricted, which disallows all scripts that weren't created in the local intranet zone or a workgroup — a deliberate security default, since scripts can carry malicious code.

questions.questionHtml: Which technology does PowerShell Remoting use instead of the older DCOM?

options.html: RDP
WinRM, built on WS-Management
SMB Direct
SSH exclusively

questions.explanationHtml: PowerShell Remoting (available since PowerShell v2) uses WinRM, which implements WS-Management — simplifying network configuration to one firewall port and encrypting all traffic.

questions.questionHtml: By default, which port does WinRM use for unencrypted HTTP traffic?
questions.explanationHtml: WinRM defaults to port 5985 for HTTP. Port 5986 is used for HTTPS, which requires additional certificate setup.

questions.questionHtml: You attempt PowerShell Remoting to a workgroup (non-domain) computer using its IP address instead of hostname. What happens?

options.html: Kerberos can't be used with an IP address, so NTLM auth is used instead — requiring the target to be listed in TrustedHosts
PowerShell Remoting refuses all IP-address connections outright
Only HTTPS connections are ever permitted to workgroup computers
WinRM automatically falls back to using DCOM

questions.explanationHtml: New-PSSession, Enter-PSSession, and Invoke-Command all accept an IP address, but Kerberos does not work with one — NTLM authentication is used instead, which means the target host must be added to the client's TrustedHosts list (or HTTPS must be used).

questions.questionHtml: Where does PowerShell store personalized aliases and functions so they persist across every new session?

options.html: They persist automatically with no configuration needed
In a PowerShell profile — a .ps1 script that runs at session start
Directly in the Windows registry, written automatically
In the $PSHOME environment variable

questions.explanationHtml: By default, aliases created interactively are lost when the session closes. To persist them, they need to be added to a PowerShell profile — a .ps1 script PowerShell checks for and runs automatically at session start.

questions.questionHtml: What does New-Item -ItemType File -Path $PROFILE -Force do?

options.html: Deletes the current profile
Creates the current user's PowerShell profile file, since none exists by default
Lists every profile path available to the host
Forces PowerShell to immediately reload its profile

questions.explanationHtml: Profiles don't exist by default — this command creates the "Current User, Current Host" profile file at the path stored in the $PROFILE automatic variable. -Force suppresses errors if intermediate folders are missing.

questions.questionHtml: Match each automatic variable to what it represents.
choices: The current object in the pipeline
Whether the last command succeeded
The exit code of the last program run
The full path to the current user's profile
questions.explanationHtml: $_ is the pipelined object, $? reports TRUE/FALSE for the last operation's success, $LASTEXITCODE holds the exit code of the last Windows-based program run, and $PROFILE stores the current profile's path — all automatic variables PowerShell maintains itself.

questions.questionHtml: Match each command alias to the cmdlet it maps to.
choices: Get-ChildItem
Get-Content
Get-Member
Where-Object
Stop-Process
questions.explanationHtml: PowerShell ships with familiar CMD/Unix-style aliases baked in: dir and ls both resolve to Get-ChildItem, type and cat resolve to Get-Content, gm to Get-Member, where to Where-Object, and kill to Stop-Process.

title: Windows Alternate Data Streams
summary: This module covers Windows Alternate Data Streams (ADS), an NTFS feature introduced in Windows NT 3.1 to implement filesystem forks for compatibility with systems like Apple's HFS+ and Novell's NWFS/NSS. ADS lets a file carry hidden alternate streams alongside its visible mainstream, and while it has legitimate uses (storing metadata, icons, thumbnails), it is also a well-documented technique for hiding data or embedding malicious code, such as a VBScript payload executed via wscript. The lesson walks through creating, viewing, and enumerating ADS on files and directories using both cmd.exe (echo, dir, type, more, notepad, certutil) and PowerShell (Get-Item, Get-Content, Set-Content, Add-Content, all with the -Stream parameter). A cyber operator needs this skill because ADS content is invisible to standard directory listings and file-viewing commands, does not change a file's MD5 hash, and can be leveraged by adversaries to hide or persist payloads on a compromised host, meaning operators must know how to enumerate and inspect streams to detect concealed data during hunt or incident-response work.

Displays the contents of a file's main stream to the console.
Writes text into a named alternate data stream (secret.info) attached to reminder.txt without altering the visible file.
Redirects an alternate data stream into the more pager to reveal its hidden content.
Opens an alternate data stream directly in Notepad as another way to view or edit hidden stream content.
Lists alternate data streams attached to a file, showing each stream's name and $DATA size.
Attempts to read an ADS with type and fails with a syntax error, demonstrating that type cannot access stream content.
Creates a new directory named kids.
Creates an alternate data stream named hidden.txt attached to a directory rather than a file.
Reveals ADS info attached to a directory, showing the hidden.txt stream on the '.' entry.
Redirects the directory's alternate data stream into the more pager, revealing the hidden top-secret information text attached to the kids directory.
PowerShell equivalent of writing text into a new file's main stream.
PowerShell's equivalent of dir; lists a file's mode, LastWriteTime, Length, and name.
Displays a file's main-stream content, PowerShell's equivalent of type.
Writes content into a named alternate data stream using PowerShell's -Stream parameter.
Lists every stream, including the main $DATA stream and any alternate data streams, attached to a file.
Retrieves the content of a specific named alternate data stream by specifying -Stream.
Filters Get-Item's stream output down to just the FileName and Stream property columns for cleaner enumeration.
Creates a benign-looking file with visible main-stream content, setting up the malicious-ADS demo.
Appends a line of VBScript logic into an alternate data stream named secret.vbs, building a hidden payload.
Reveals the payload hidden inside the secret.vbs alternate data stream.
Runs VBScript code stored inside an alternate data stream via Windows Script Host, demonstrating ADS-based code execution.

Computes the MD5 hash of test.txt's main stream; run once before and once after editing the secret.vbs stream, both times returning the same hash, to prove that editing an ADS does not change the file hash.

terms.description: An NTFS feature allowing a file or directory to carry additional named streams of data beyond its default visible content; not shown by standard directory listings or file-viewing commands.
Microsoft's native Windows filesystem, which stores files as a combination of attributes, security settings, a mainstream, and any alternate streams.
Apple's legacy filesystem that supports resource forks; cited as one of the systems Microsoft aimed for compatibility with when it built ADS into NTFS.
Novell's original filesystem, referenced as another fork-supporting filesystem that motivated NTFS's alternate stream design.
Novell's later filesystem, also cited alongside NWFS as a system ADS was designed to interoperate with.

The NTFS attribute type that stores a stream's actual content: every file has one unnamed $DATA attribute holding its main-stream content, plus one named $DATA attribute per alternate stream. Only the unnamed main stream's $DATA feeds into a file's hash.
A hashing algorithm used via certutil in the lesson to fingerprint a file's main stream; the demo shows ADS edits leave the MD5 hash unchanged.
The scripting language used to write the payload hidden inside the secret.vbs alternate data stream in the lesson's malicious-ADS demo.
The Windows subsystem (invoked via wscript) used to execute the VBScript code stored in an alternate data stream, demonstrating ADS as a code-execution vector.
A built-in Windows command-line tool for certificate and hash operations; used in the lesson via -hashfile to compute a file's MD5 hash.
A built-in Windows security feature noted in the lesson as being ADS-aware, meaning it can scan alternate data stream content for threats.
An older Windows filesystem that does not support multiple data streams; alternate data streams are stripped when a file is copied onto a FAT32 volume.

facts: ADS was first introduced to NTFS in Windows NT 3.1 as Microsoft's attempt at implementing filesystem forks for compatibility with Apple's HFS+ and Novell's NWFS and NSS.
In NTFS, files consist of attributes, security settings, a mainstream, and alternate streams, but by default only the mainstream is visible.
ADS has legitimate uses, such as storing metadata like file attributes, icons, and image thumbnails.
Alternate data streams can be scanned by antivirus software, and Windows Defender SmartScreen is ADS-aware.
Adding or modifying an alternate data stream does not change a file's MD5 hash; only altering the main stream ($DATA) changes the hash.
Alternate data stream content is deleted if a file is copied to a FAT32 volume, since FAT32 does not support multiple streams.
ADS cannot be disabled on NTFS.
The naming syntax for an alternate data stream is [filename.extension]:[alternate_stream_name]:$DATA.
Commands like dir and type show no visible difference in a file after an alternate data stream is added to it.
The type command cannot read ADS content directly and instead returns a syntax-incorrect error.
dir /R reveals the presence and size of alternate data streams attached to files or directories.
Alternate data streams can be attached to directories, not just files.
In PowerShell, Set-Content and Add-Content with the -Stream parameter write to a named ADS, while Get-Content -Stream reads its content.
Get-Item file -Stream * lists every stream on a file, including the main $DATA stream and any alternate data streams.
Malicious logic, such as VBScript, can be hidden in an alternate data stream and executed with wscript.
Because ADS-hidden code doesn't change a file's visible content or its main-stream hash, an operator cannot assume a file is untampered with just because its hash is unchanged.

questions.questionHtml: In what Windows version was Alternate Data Streams (ADS) first introduced into NTFS, and why?

options.html: Windows NT 3.1, as Microsoft's attempt at implementing filesystem forks for compatibility with filesystems like Apple's HFS+ and Novell's NWFS/NSS
Windows XP, to support long file names on FAT32
Windows 7, to enable BitLocker encryption metadata
Windows 2000, as part of the Active Directory schema

questions.explanationHtml: ADS was first introduced to NTFS in Windows NT 3.1 as Microsoft's attempt at implementing filesystem forks, done to maintain compatibility with other filesystems like Apple's HFS+ and Novell's NWFS and NSS.

questions.questionHtml: According to the lesson, what does an NTFS file consist of?

options.html: Attributes, security settings, a mainstream, and alternate streams
A master boot record, partition table, and file allocation table
An inode number, permission bits, and a single data fork
A registry hive, a security descriptor, and a symbolic link

questions.explanationHtml: In NTFS, files consist of attributes, security settings, a mainstream, and alternate streams.

questions.questionHtml: By default, which part of an NTFS file's data is visible when browsing normally (e.g., with dir or File Explorer)?

options.html: Only the mainstream
Only the alternate streams
Both the mainstream and all alternate streams equally
Neither; both require special third-party software

questions.explanationHtml: By default, only the mainstream is visible. Alternate streams stay hidden unless specifically queried.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following correctly represents the syntax used to reference an Alternate Data Stream?

options.html: [filename.extension]:[alternate_stream_name]:$DATA
[alternate_stream_name]@[filename.extension]#$DATA
$DATA:[filename.extension]:[alternate_stream_name]
[filename.extension]/[alternate_stream_name]/$DATA

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson gives the syntax as [filename.extension]:[alternate_stream_name]:$DATA.

questions.questionHtml: Besides hiding data, what legitimate purpose has ADS historically served on NTFS?

options.html: Storing metadata such as file attributes, icons, and image thumbnails
Storing the entire Windows Registry
Storing user account passwords in plaintext
Storing the NTFS master file table (MFT)

questions.explanationHtml: ADS has been used to store metadata, like file attributes, icons, and image thumbnails, in addition to being a great way to hide data.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements about Alternate Data Streams are TRUE, according to the lesson? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Windows Defender Smartscreen is ADS-aware and can scan stream content
Writing to or altering an ADS does not change the file's MD5 hash
An ADS is deleted if the file is copied to a FAT32 volume
ADS support cannot be disabled on NTFS
ADS can only be created on files, never on directories
ADS content is automatically encrypted by BitLocker

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states ADS can be scanned by antivirus (Smartscreen is ADS aware), does not change the MD5 hash, is deleted once copied to FAT32, and cannot be disabled. It also demonstrates ADS on a directory (the kids example), so ADS is not file-only. BitLocker encryption of ADS is never mentioned.

questions.questionHtml: In Command Prompt, which command correctly creates an Alternate Data Stream named secret.info on reminder.txt?

options.html: echo social security numbers > reminder.txt:secret.info
copy reminder.txt secret.info
type reminder.txt > secret.info
attrib +h reminder.txt:secret.info

questions.explanationHtml: Piping echo output to filename:streamname is exactly how the lesson creates an ADS in CMD.

questions.questionHtml: What does running dir /R reminder.txt accomplish that a plain dir reminder.txt does not?

options.html: It displays the names and sizes of any Alternate Data Streams attached to the file, without showing their contents
It recursively lists ADS content for every file in the directory
It removes all Alternate Data Streams from the file
It repairs a corrupted ADS

questions.explanationHtml: dir /R displays ADS info like reminder.txt:secret.info:$DATA, which proves a stream exists and its size, but this is not the same as listing the ADS contents.

questions.questionHtml: An analyst runs type reminder.txt:secret.info in Command Prompt. What happens?

options.html: CMD returns an error: 'The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect.'
It prints the ADS content to the screen exactly like more does
It silently deletes the ADS
It converts the ADS into the mainstream

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson shows that type is unable to list ADS content and instead returns 'The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect.'

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following commands successfully displays the contents of an Alternate Data Stream in Command Prompt, per the lesson's demonstration?

options.html: more < reminder.txt:secret.info
type reminder.txt:secret.info
dir reminder.txt:secret.info
attrib reminder.txt:secret.info

questions.explanationHtml: more < reminder.txt:secret.info reads the ADS content into more, showing the hidden text. notepad reminder.txt:secret.info works too, but type fails with a syntax error.

questions.questionHtml: Can Alternate Data Streams be attached to directories, not just files?

options.html: Yes — the lesson demonstrates creating kids:hidden.txt on a directory named kids, visible as .:hidden.txt:$DATA with dir /R
No — ADS is a file-only feature; directories cannot carry streams
Only on FAT32-formatted directories
Only if the directory is compressed first

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson's directory demo creates a kids directory, writes an ADS called kids:hidden.txt onto it, and confirms it with dir /R kids and more < kids:hidden.txt.

questions.questionHtml: After creating an ADS on reminder.txt with Set-Content -Stream, what does Get-ChildItem reminder.txt show?

options.html: No visible change — the file's Length and other listed attributes look the same as before the ADS was added
A new file listed in the directory named reminder.txt:secret.info
An error, because Get-ChildItem cannot process files containing streams
The full content of the ADS printed below the file name

questions.explanationHtml: Just like dir in CMD, Get-ChildItem shows no visible change to reminder.txt even after an ADS has been added to it.

questions.questionHtml: What does running Get-Item reminder.txt -Stream * do?

options.html: Lists every stream on reminder.txt, including the mainstream (:$DATA) and any alternate streams, with properties like FileName, Stream, and Length
Deletes all streams except the mainstream
Opens all streams simultaneously in Notepad
Renames every alternate stream to $DATA

questions.explanationHtml: Get-Item -Stream * enumerates all streams on the file. The mainstream's Stream property shows :$DATA, while the ADS's Stream property shows its given name, e.g. secret.info.

questions.questionHtml: In the lesson's malicious ADS demonstration, which command executes the code stored in the stream test.txt:secret.vbs?

options.html: wscript .\test.txt:secret.vbs
Get-Content .\test.txt:secret.vbs
Set-Content .\test.txt:secret.vbs -Execute
certutil -hashfile test.txt:secret.vbs

questions.explanationHtml: wscript, part of Windows Script Host, runs the code contained in test.txt:secret.vbs directly.

questions.questionHtml: An operator edits the content of test.txt:secret.vbs with Notepad, then re-runs certutil -hashfile test.txt MD5. What does the lesson say happens to the file's hash?

options.html: It remains unchanged, because hashing reflects only the mainstream ($DATA); ADS content is not included
It changes immediately, proving the ADS was tampered with
certutil refuses to hash a file that contains an ADS
The hash changes only if the ADS is larger than the mainstream

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson explicitly states that changing the ADS content of a file does not affect the file hash; only changing the actual content on the main stream ($DATA) results in a hash change. This means an operator cannot assume a file was not tampered with just because its hash has not changed.

title: Linux Essentials
summary: Linux Essentials introduces the Bash command-line shell that cyber operators rely on immediately after gaining access to a Linux system, since the CLI offers three advantages a GUI cannot match: speed, scaling, and automation. This module covers running commands with arguments, variables and command substitution, redirecting the standard input/output/error streams, chaining commands with pipes, automating repetitive work with for/if/while, navigating the Linux File System Hierarchy, and the user/group rwx and octal permission model that governs what a given account can read, write, or execute. It closes with the core text-processing toolkit — grep, awk, and sed — used to slice through command output and log files for the signal that matters.

commands.description: Prints the current working directory.
Shows the username currently logged in as — key situational awareness right after gaining access to a system.
Sets a variable without a dollar sign, then reads it back with one.
Command substitution — assigns the output of ls / to a variable instead of a literal string.
Pipes the recursive listing of /etc into grep, filtering the output down to lines mentioning syslog.
Redirects only standard error (stream 2) to the null device, silencing error output while keeping stdout visible.
Appends a command's output to an existing file instead of overwriting it.

commands.command: for item in $objects; do echo $item; done
commands.description: Iterates a collection assigned to a variable, running a command against each item until the collection is exhausted.
Hex-dumps a file's raw bytes, used in the lesson to read the ELF file signature at the start of the ls binary.
Sets rwx permissions using octal notation (Read=4, Write=2, Execute=1 per User/Group/Others set), e.g. 7 = full rwx.
Reformats/selects specific whitespace-delimited fields from piped text, e.g. to build a CSV from an ls -l listing.
Stream editor — rewrites matching text as it passes through to standard output.

terms.description: A text-based interface offering three advantages over a GUI, per the lesson: speed (fewer resources consumed), scaling (multiple commands run at once with enough expertise), and automation (scripts handle repetitive tasks).
The three numbered I/O streams every command uses: stdin is 0, stdout is 1, and stderr is 2 — the default destination for a failed command's error output.

questions.questionHtml: According to the Linux File System Hierarchy (FSH), what is stored in /etc?

options.html: Host-specific system configurations such as network settings, daemons, and firewall rules.
Essential user commands like ls and echo.
Home directories for every non-root user.
The system's log files.

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson describes /etc as standing for "everything configurable" and containing network configurations, system services (daemons), firewall configurations, etc.

questions.questionHtml: Match each Linux File System Hierarchy location to what it contains.
choices: Root of the file system — everything starts from this directory
Essential user commands like ls and echo, usable by every user
Directories for every non-root user, each with a home directory and login shell
Host-specific configuration such as network settings, daemons, and firewall rules
Variable data, including system logs by default
questions.explanationHtml: The Linux FSH defines / as the root of the filesystem, /bin for essential commands, /home for user directories, /etc for host-specific configuration, and /var for variable data such as logs.

questions.questionHtml: Running xxd on the ls binary reveals the hex sequence 7f45 4c46 at the very start of the file. What does this file signature indicate?

options.html: The file is in the ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) file format, unique to Linux/Unix executables.
The file is a plain-text configuration file.
The file is corrupted and cannot be executed.
The file is a compressed archive.

questions.explanationHtml: The signature 7f45 4c46 (bytes \x7fELF) marks the file as being in the ELF file format — the standard executable format on Linux/Unix systems, which tells the OS how to load and run it. File signatures, usually found in a file's first few bytes, tell the OS how to use it.

questions.questionHtml: In an /etc/passwd entry such as student:x:1001:1001::/home/student:/bin/bash, what does the x in the second field indicate?

options.html: That an encrypted password for the user is stored in the /etc/shadow file.
That the account has been disabled.
That the user has root privileges.
That the field is unused and reserved for future versions of Linux.

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson explains that an x character indicates that an encrypted password is stored in the /etc/shadow file.

questions.questionHtml: Read, Write, and Execute permissions have the numeric (octal) values 4, 2, and 1 respectively. What octal value represents a permission group with full Read, Write, and Execute access?
questions.explanationHtml: Read (4) + Write (2) + Execute (1) = 7, the octal representation of full rwx permissions for a given User, Group, or Others permission set.

questions.questionHtml: A user has read permission on a file itself, but does NOT have read permission on the directory that contains it. According to the lesson, can the user read the file's contents?

options.html: No — file permissions do not override directory permissions, so the file still cannot be read.
Yes — file permissions always take precedence over directory permissions.
Yes, but only if the user is a member of the file's owning group.
It depends only on whether the sticky bit is set on the directory.

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states: file permissions do not overrule directory permissions. If a user does not have read rights to a directory, it also cannot read any of its files even if the file's permissions allow it.

questions.questionHtml: What does the sticky bit special permission do?

options.html: It removes the ability to delete files in a directory unless the user attempting the deletion is the file's owner (root can still delete).
It forces every file in the directory to run with root permissions.
It prevents any user, including the owner, from deleting files in the directory.
It grants write access to the directory for every user on the system.

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson explains the sticky bit addresses the problem of anyone with write access to a shared directory (like /var/tmp) being able to delete any file in it: the sticky bit removes the ability to delete files unless the user attempting is the owner of the file, though root can still delete the file.

questions.questionHtml: The lesson shows /bin/ping with permissions -rwsr-xr-x, where the owner's execute bit is replaced with s. What does this SUID bit do?

options.html: It forces the executable to run with the permissions of its owning user (root, in this case), rather than the user who launched it.
It prevents the executable from ever being run by a non-root user.
It hides the executable from an ls -l listing.
It marks the file as a symbolic link.

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states: when an executable is run in Linux, it runs with the permissions of the user who started it. However, SUID and SGID change that to force the executable to run as the owning user or group. This is shown as an s in the user (SUID) or group (SGID) field of ls -l.

questions.questionHtml: What does the awk command primarily do, as described in the lesson?

options.html: Reformats or selects specific sections/fields of text based on a delimiter, such as pulling out columns to build a CSV file.
Searches text for patterns using regular expressions.
Edits text in place as it streams to standard output.
Displays manual pages for other commands.

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson describes awk as a tool that allows you to reformat or select sections of text based on delimiters, for example ls -l /etc | awk -F " " '{print$3","$4","$9}' to build a comma-delimited file from specific columns.

Reformats or selects sections of text based on a delimiter, e.g. building a CSV from specific fields

title: Windows Boot Process
summary: This module (Lesson 112-CCTC05) walks through the Windows boot process end to end — from BIOS/UEFI firmware initialization and the MBR/GPT boot sector, through kernel load and initialization (ntoskrnl.exe, hal.dll), through the Session 0/Session 1 subsystem startup, to the LogonUi.exe credential prompt. It also covers hands-on use of the bcdedit command to inspect, back up, and modify Boot Configuration Data, and shows how to inspect the Service Control Manager's registry keys and running services with sc, reg, and tasklist. A cyber operator needs this because the boot chain is a prime target for rootkits and bootkits, which load before anti-malware software does and can persist with SYSTEM-level privileges by hijacking boot drivers, services, or startup registry keys; knowing the legitimate sequence (bootmgr/winload/smss/wininit/services.exe/winlogon) is what lets an analyst recognize when that sequence has been tampered with.

Adds the {ntldr} entry to the front of the boot menu display order.
Forcibly deletes the legacy {ntldr} boot loader entry from the BCD store.

terms.description: Legacy firmware that initializes critical hardware (SATA devices, display adapters, SDRAM) and then locates the disk's MBR to hand off to the boot loader.
Modern firmware that replaces BIOS; it boots faster, lives in flash/EEPROM for easy updates, supports Secure Boot (only verified drivers load), and supports drives up to 9 zettabytes.
The disk sector a BIOS system locates after hardware checks; it holds partition data and the code that starts the first-stage boot loader (NTLDR or bootmgr).
The modern partitioning scheme a UEFI system reads (via the EFI system partition) in place of the MBR used by BIOS.
The store of boot settings — read from \Boot\BCD on BIOS or the EFI system partition on UEFI — that tells bootmgr/bootmgfw.efi where to find winload.
The command-line tool used to view, export/import, and modify BCD boot entries, including description, device, path, display order, timeout, and safeboot values.
The boot loader used by Windows 2003 and older to take over from the MBR and start the operating system. NTLDR predates BCD and reads boot.ini, not \Boot\BCD.
The boot loader used on BIOS systems since Windows 7 SP1; it reads \Boot\BCD to locate winload.exe.
Loads essential disk drivers plus the Windows kernel (ntoskrnl.exe) and its dependencies; the .exe form runs under BIOS and the .efi form runs under UEFI.
Reads saved hibernation data from hiberfil.sys to restore a previous Windows session instead of performing a cold boot.
The core Windows kernel file; once loaded it loads the registry and device drivers, starts the pagefile, loads hal.dll, and spawns the System process.
Provides the abstraction between hardware interfaces and ntoskrnl.exe so the kernel does not need to address hardware directly.
Loads environment variables such as %APPDATA% and %COMPUTERNAME%, populates the pagefile, and starts the kernel/user subsystems along with a csrss.exe per session.
Supports process and thread creation and management; a separate instance runs in every session.
Provides user authentication, enforces local security policy, and generates access tokens; started in Session 0 by wininit.exe.
Loads AutoStart services in Session 0, calling on LSASS to authenticate services configured to run as an account other than System.

Session 0 isolates high-privilege system services (running as SYSTEM); Session 1 and higher are standard interactive user desktop sessions, each with its own csrss.exe, winlogon.exe, userinit.exe, and explorer.exe.

terms.full: Firmware, Bootkit, Kernel, and Driver Rootkits
terms.description: Malware classes that hide by loading before or alongside the OS: firmware rootkits overwrite BIOS/firmware, bootkits replace the OS bootloader, kernel rootkits replace part of the kernel, and driver rootkits impersonate a boot driver.

facts: The Windows boot process is broken into three high-level stages: hardware initialization, loading the boot sector or boot manager, and loading the operating system from the boot sector.
Rootkits target the boot process because traditional anti-malware software does not load until after the kernel and boot drivers have already started.

UEFI boots faster than BIOS, is typically stored in flash memory or EEPROM for easier patching, offers Secure Boot to allow only verified drivers, and supports drives up to 9 zettabytes versus BIOS's 2-terabyte limit.
Running "bcdedit | findstr /i winload" reveals whether a system is BIOS or UEFI: winload.exe indicates BIOS and winload.efi indicates UEFI.
Msinfo32.exe's BIOS Mode field can also reveal the boot mode; a value of "Legacy" means the hardware is UEFI-capable but currently running in BIOS compatibility mode.
On BIOS systems, bootmgr reads \Boot\BCD to locate winload.exe; on UEFI systems, bootmgfw.efi reads the BCD in the EFI system partition to locate winload.efi.
Winresume.exe restores a previously hibernated Windows session by reading hiberfil.sys.
After ntoskrnl.exe loads the registry, device drivers, the pagefile, and hal.dll, it spawns the System process, which in turn spawns the session management processes smss.exe and csrss.exe.
The user subsystem, which runs in Session 0 and Session 1, is the first part of the Windows boot process a user can directly manipulate.
Session 0 processes run with SYSTEM-level privileges, which exceed those of an administrative account, making Session 0 services a documented MITRE ATT&CK attack surface.
wininit.exe initializes Session 0 by starting lsm.exe, lsass.exe, and services.exe.

Session 1 and higher spawn a per-session csrss.exe, then winlogon.exe (which prompts for credentials via logonui.exe), then userinit.exe (which creates the account token and user environment), and finally explorer.exe as the desktop shell.
Every autostart service's configuration lives under the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services, which can be queried with the reg command.
The bcdedit command can back up and restore the entire BCD store with /export and /import, and can create, modify, reorder, or delete individual boot loader entries by referencing their {identifier}.
Setting a boot entry's safeboot value to "minimal" with bcdedit forces that entry into Safe Mode on the next boot.
A healthy system should show exactly one Windows Boot Manager entry; more than one boot loader entry present indicates a dual-boot configuration.

questions.questionHtml: What are the three phases of the Windows boot process, in order?

options.html: Hardware Initialization → Loading the Boot Sector or Boot Manager → Loading the Operating System from the Boot Sector
Loading the Operating System → Hardware Initialization → Loading the Boot Manager
Loading the Boot Manager → Loading the Operating System → Hardware Initialization
Initializing the Kernel → Hardware Initialization → Starting Session 0

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson breaks the boot process into three steps: Hardware Initialization, Loading the Boot Sector or Boot Manager, and Loading the Operating System from the Boot Sector.

questions.questionHtml: Why do rootkits so often target the earliest parts of the boot process?

options.html: Because anti-malware software traditionally doesn't load until after the kernel and boot drivers do, letting a rootkit start first
Because the boot process always runs with lower privileges than antivirus software
Because Windows disables all security logging during boot
Because BCDEdit cannot detect any changes made before Session 1 starts

questions.explanationHtml: Anti-malware traditionally doesn't load until after the kernel and boot drivers do — exactly the gap rootkits are built to exploit. They run in kernel mode with the same privileges as the OS and can sometimes start before it.

questions.questionHtml: Match each rootkit type to what it overwrites or replaces.
choices: The PC's BIOS or other hardware firmware, so it starts before the OS even loads
The OS bootloader, to load the bootkit before the OS
A portion of the OS kernel, to start when the OS loads
A boot driver the OS uses to communicate with the PC
questions.explanationHtml: Firmware rootkits overwrite BIOS/firmware; bootkits replace the OS bootloader; kernel rootkits replace part of the kernel; driver rootkits pretend to be a boot driver used to communicate with the PC.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is NOT listed in the lesson as a benefit of UEFI over BIOS?

options.html: UEFI boots much faster than BIOS systems, especially for Windows machines
UEFI firmware is usually loaded into flash memory or EEPROM, making it easier to update and patch
UEFI offers Secured Boot mode which only allows verified drivers to load
UEFI requires significantly more system RAM than BIOS to operate

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson lists faster boot, easier updates via flash/EEPROM, Secured Boot, and support for drives up to 9 zettabytes as UEFI's benefits. It never mentions RAM requirements.

questions.questionHtml: Match each boot-chain term to its description.
choices: Found by BIOS after hardware checks; contains disk partitions and the first-stage boot loader code
Found by UEFI; the EFI Partition that contains UEFI Boot Managers
The boot loader used on Windows 2003 and older
The boot loader used on Windows 7 Service Pack 1 and newer (BIOS systems)
questions.explanationHtml: BIOS locates the MBR, which contains the disk partitions and boot loader code. UEFI instead reads the EFI Partition, which holds the UEFI Boot Managers. NTLDR was used on Windows 2003 and older; bootmgr replaced it starting with Windows 7 SP1.

questions.questionHtml: On a UEFI system, which file in the EFI Partition acts as the Windows Boot Manager and hands off to the operating system?

options.html: bootmgfw.efi
bootmgr
winload.exe
ntoskrnl.exe

questions.explanationHtml: The EFI Partition contains UEFI Boot Managers — on Windows this is bootmgfw.efi (Windows Boot Manager), which takes over and starts the operating system.

questions.questionHtml: An operator runs bcdedit | findstr /i winload and the output shows winload.efi. What does this tell them about the machine's firmware?

options.html: It is running UEFI
It is running legacy BIOS
It is currently resuming from hibernation
It has a corrupted Boot Configuration Data store

questions.explanationHtml: winload.exe indicates BIOS; winload.efi indicates UEFI. Filtering bcdedit output for "winload" is one documented way to tell the two apart.

questions.questionHtml: Besides bcdedit, which built-in GUI tool can confirm whether a system is running BIOS or UEFI by checking its "BIOS Mode" field?

options.html: Msinfo32.exe
Regedit.exe
Tasklist
Services.msc

questions.explanationHtml: Msinfo32.exe's System Summary includes a BIOS Mode field. "Legacy" there means the system is UEFI-compatible but currently running in BIOS-compatibility mode.

questions.questionHtml: Which TWO of the following are tasks that winload.exe / winload.efi performs while loading the Windows kernel?

options.html: Loads essential drivers required to read data from disk
Loads the Windows kernel (ntoskrnl.exe) and its dependencies
Prompts the user for logon credentials
Populates the pagefile with environmental variables

questions.explanationHtml: winload loads the essential drivers needed to read from disk, then loads the Windows kernel (ntoskrnl.exe) and its dependencies. Prompting for credentials is logonui.exe's job (Session 1), and populating the pagefile with environment variables is part of smss.exe's job.

questions.questionHtml: What is the purpose of hal.dll, which Ntoskrnl.exe loads while initializing the kernel?

options.html: It provides abstraction between hardware interfaces and Ntoskrnl.exe
It stores the Boot Configuration Data (BCD)
It authenticates users and issues access tokens
It renders the Windows desktop and Start menu

questions.explanationHtml: hal.dll (the Hardware Abstraction Layer) provides abstraction between hardware interfaces and Ntoskrnl.exe.

questions.questionHtml: Which file does winresume.exe read to restore a previous Windows instance instead of performing a normal boot?

options.html: hiberfil.sys
pagefile.sys
Setupact.log
The BCD store

questions.explanationHtml: Winresume.exe reads previously saved data from hiberfil.sys (hibernation mode) to restore a previous Windows instance.

questions.questionHtml: Once the Windows kernel finishes loading, what does it spawn first, which then spawns smss.exe and csrss.exe?

options.html: The System process
wininit.exe
winlogon.exe
explorer.exe

questions.explanationHtml: Once the kernel is done loading it spawns System, which hosts kernel-mode-only threads (like drivers). System then spawns the session management processes smss.exe and csrss.exe.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following best describes smss.exe, the Session Manager Subsystem?

options.html: It loads environmental variables, populates the pagefile, and starts the kernel and user mode subsystems
It prompts the user for logon credentials via a GUI
It authenticates users and generates access tokens
It loads AutoStart services on behalf of the Service Control Manager

questions.explanationHtml: smss.exe loads environmental variables like %APPDATA% and %COMPUTERNAME%, populates the pagefile, starts the kernel and user mode subsystems, and starts a csrss.exe for each user subsystem.

questions.questionHtml: Why does Windows run services and other high-privilege processes in Session 0 instead of alongside regular user processes?

options.html: To isolate them from individual users' processes
Because Session 0 has no access to the registry
Because only Session 0 can load device drivers
Because Session 1 is reserved exclusively for the SYSTEM account

questions.explanationHtml: Session 0 is for security and high-privilege processes such as services; they run in a separate session specifically to isolate them from individual users' processes.

questions.questionHtml: Why are processes in Session 0 a notable attack surface for a cyber operator?

options.html: They run as SYSTEM, a higher privilege than any administrative account, and can be tricked into executing malicious commands via services
They are the only processes visible to tasklist
They automatically disable Windows Defender
They run with lower privileges than any Session 1 process

questions.explanationHtml: Session 0 processes are created with SYSTEM, the highest permission level in Windows — higher than an administrative account — and represent the OS itself. They can be tricked into executing malicious commands via services.

questions.questionHtml: In Session 1's startup order, which process is spawned right after that session's csrss.exe, and by default prompts for credentials using logonui.exe?

options.html: Winlogon.exe
userinit.exe
explorer.exe
lsass.exe

questions.explanationHtml: Session 1's order is: spawn Session 1's csrss.exe, spawn Winlogon.exe (which by default prompts for credentials with logonui.exe), spawn userinit.exe (creates an account token and a custom environment), then spawn explorer.exe as the graphical shell.

questions.questionHtml: Which bcdedit switch backs up the current Boot Configuration Data (BCD) store to a file so it can be restored later with /import?

options.html: /export
/set
/create
/displayorder

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson demo shows bcdedit /export C:\Lion_BCD to back up the current BCD settings, and bcdedit /import C:\Lion_BCD to restore them.

questions.questionHtml: According to the lesson, what does it mean if bcdedit shows more than one Windows Boot Loader entry?

options.html: It indicates a dual-boot system
The BCD store is corrupted and must be rebuilt
The machine has more than one Windows Boot Manager, which is expected
Hibernation mode is currently active

questions.explanationHtml: Per the lesson, there should only ever be one Windows Boot Manager, but more than one Windows Boot Loader entry indicates a dual-boot system; the default entry is what loads if no user selection is made.

title: Linux Boot Process
summary: This module traces the Linux boot process end-to-end: firmware (BIOS/UEFI) hands off to a first-stage bootloader (MBR or GPT), which loads the second-stage GRUB bootloader, which loads the Linux kernel, which spawns an init system (legacy SysV or modern systemd) that brings the machine to a target run level, followed by post-boot shell environment files that run at login. Along the way the lesson teaches supporting forensic skills — reading hexadecimal addresses and hex dumps — needed to inspect raw boot sectors like the MBR with tools such as xxd and dd. A cyber operator needs this material because every stage (firmware, bootloader, kernel modules, init scripts, systemd units, shell startup files) is a potential point where a skilled adversary can persist, hide, or subvert the system, and because a locked-down system requires understanding the configuration options available at each layer. The lesson grounds each concept in real commands run on a Linux operations station (lsblk, xxd, dd, file, cat, ltrace, lsmod, ls, systemctl) so students can both configure and audit a Linux system's boot chain.

facts: The boot process is a defined sequence of stages that brings a computer from off to fully functional, and a skilled adversary who understands each stage can alter it to further their goals.
BIOS and UEFI are firmware, not software, stored in non-volatile memory (such as flash memory on the motherboard); both run and hand off control to the bootloader before Linux itself starts.
UEFI improves on BIOS by booting faster, offering Secured Boot mode (only verified drivers load), and supporting drives up to 9 zettabytes versus BIOS's 2-terabyte limit.
The Master Boot Record occupies the first 512 bytes of a hard drive: 446 bytes of bootstrap code, four 16-byte primary partition entries, and a 2-byte boot signature (0x55 0xAA).
Linux identifies a file as an MBR by its file signature located at hex addresses 0x00 and 0x01.

On legacy MBR systems, GRUB loads in stages: boot.img (Stage 1) sits in the MBR's first 440 bytes, core.img (Stage 1.5) sits between the bootstrap and the first partition, and normal.mod (Stage 2) reads /boot/grub/grub.cfg to display available kernels.
On UEFI/GPT systems, GRUB Stage 1 is instead the file grubx64.efi, located on an EFI partition or in /boot.

GPT is the modern replacement for MBR: it works only with UEFI, stores redundant boot sectors across the disk, supports 128 or more partitions versus MBR's 4, and supports partitions up to 9 zettabytes.
The Linux kernel is a monolithic kernel that controls memory management, device management, I/O request handling, and CPU process scheduling, with every system action occurring through a system call.
Linux kernel modules extend the kernel's base functionality without requiring a rebuild, and if a module fails, only its dependent functionality stops while the rest of the system keeps running.
Once loaded, the kernel is hard-coded to execute /sbin/init, which starts one of two initialization daemon families: legacy SysV or modern systemd.
In SysV, /etc/inittab's initdefault entry sets the default run level (0-6), and if that run level fails to start, the machine falls back to executing the scripts in run level 0 (halt).
SysV run-level scripts in /etc/rc#.d are symbolic links into /etc/init.d, named with an S (start) or K (kill) prefix followed by a two-digit number that determines execution order.

In systemd, the kernel spawns /sbin/init (symlinked to /lib/systemd/systemd), and target units such as graphical.target replace SysV run levels, with default.target itself symlinked to the active target (e.g., graphical.target).
A systemd target's Requires= dependency must succeed for the calling target to execute, while a Wants= dependency can fail without stopping the calling target.
Systemd searches at least eleven separate filesystem locations for a target's want/require dependencies, so checking only one or two directories will miss dependencies.
The getty program (started by init) displays a login prompt on each virtual console, and once a login name is given it invokes /bin/login to prompt for and verify a password.

/etc/environment sets global variables for every user and process and is read only once when Init completes, so any change requires a full system restart to take effect, whereas /etc/profile runs on every interactive login and .bashrc runs on every interactive non-login shell.

questions.questionHtml: What is the correct high-level order of the Linux boot process?

options.html: BIOS/UEFI → 1st Stage Bootloader (MBR/GPT) → 2nd Stage Bootloader (GRUB) → Kernel → Init → Post Boot
Kernel → BIOS/UEFI → GRUB → Init → MBR/GPT → Post Boot
Init → BIOS/UEFI → Kernel → GRUB → MBR/GPT → Post Boot
GRUB → MBR/GPT → BIOS/UEFI → Init → Kernel → Post Boot

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson lays out the boot process as a sequence of stages: firmware (BIOS/UEFI) checks hardware and locates the MBR or GPT, the 1st stage bootloader hands off to GRUB (2nd stage bootloader), GRUB loads the Linux Kernel, the kernel spawns Init, and finally Post Boot scripts configure the user shell environment.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary job of the BIOS/UEFI firmware during boot?

options.html: Ensure critical hardware (SATA devices, display adapters, SDRAM) is functional, then locate the MBR or GPT
Load the Linux kernel directly into memory
Read /etc/inittab to determine the run level
Execute /etc/profile.d scripts for the logging-in user

questions.explanationHtml: BIOS and UEFI are firmware that ensure critical hardware is functional, then locate the MBR (Master Boot Record) or GPT (GUID Partition Table). The BIOS runs and exits before the Linux system even starts.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following are true advantages of UEFI over legacy BIOS, according to the lesson? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: UEFI boots much faster than BIOS systems, especially for Windows machines
UEFI firmware is usually loaded into flash memory or EEPROM, making it easier to update and patch
UEFI offers Secured Boot mode, which only allows verified drivers to load
UEFI supports drives up to 9 zettabytes, versus 2 terabytes for BIOS
UEFI eliminates the need for a 2nd stage bootloader like GRUB

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson lists four UEFI benefits: faster boot, easier firmware updates via flash/EEPROM, Secured Boot (verified drivers only), and support for drives up to 9 zettabytes versus 2 terabytes for BIOS. GRUB is still used as the 2nd stage bootloader in UEFI/GPT systems (e.g., grubx64.efi).

questions.questionHtml: According to the lesson, what is the difference between firmware and volatile memory behavior?

options.html: Firmware lives in non-volatile memory that does not clear itself after a restart, unlike volatile memory
Firmware lives in volatile memory that clears itself after every restart
Firmware and software are the same thing, stored identically
Firmware is only found in RAM (SDRAM)

questions.explanationHtml: Firmware is software coded into non-volatile memory devices (ROM, EPROM, EEPROM, Flash memory). Non-volatile memory does not clear itself after a restart, while volatile memory does.

questions.questionHtml: What is the role of the 1st Stage Bootloader (MBR or GPT)?

options.html: It locates and finishes loading the 2nd stage bootloader known as GRUB
It loads the Linux kernel directly into memory
It executes /sbin/init to start the initialization daemon
It reads /etc/environment to set global variables

questions.explanationHtml: 1st Stage Bootloaders are the MBR and GPT because they are the first part of loading an operating system. They locate and finish loading the 2nd stage bootloader known as GRUB.

questions.questionHtml: How many bytes make up the Master Boot Record, and how many of those are Bootstrap Code?

options.html: 512 bytes total; 446 bytes are Bootstrap Code
1024 bytes total; 512 bytes are Bootstrap Code
256 bytes total; 128 bytes are Bootstrap Code
512 bytes total; 512 bytes are Bootstrap Code

questions.explanationHtml: The first 512 bytes of a hard drive contain the MBR: 446 bytes of Bootstrap Code Area, four 16-byte partition entries (64 bytes total), and a 2-byte boot signature (0x55 0xAA) — totaling 512 bytes.

questions.questionHtml: How many primary partition entries does an MBR support, and what is the boot signature value at the end of the MBR?

options.html: 4 partition entries; boot signature 0x55 0xAA
128 partition entries; boot signature 0x55 0xAA
4 partition entries; boot signature 0xEB 0x63
8 partition entries; boot signature 0xFF 0xFF

questions.explanationHtml: The MBR layout has 4 partition entries (0x01BE, 0x01CE, 0x01DE, 0x01EE), each 16 bytes, and ends at 0x01FF with the 2-byte boot signature 0x55 0xAA. GPT, by contrast, supports 128+ partitions.

questions.questionHtml: In the lesson's lsblk example, what does sda1 represent, and how is it mounted?

options.html: Virtual disk A's partition 1, mounted as the / (root) drive in Linux
A loopback device mounted at /snap/core18
A read-only optical drive mounted at /media/student
The MBR boot sector itself

questions.explanationHtml: In the lesson's lsblk output, sda is the virtual disk, and sda1 is that disk's first partition, mounted as / (the root drive).

questions.questionHtml: Compared to MBR, which statements about GPT (GUID Partition Table) are true according to the lesson?

options.html: GPT stores redundant boot sectors around the disk, supports up to 128+ partitions, and requires UEFI firmware
GPT only supports 4 partitions and works with either BIOS or UEFI
GPT is a legacy standard rarely used on modern machines
GPT stores the bootstrap code in the same 446-byte area as MBR

questions.explanationHtml: GPT only works with UEFI firmware, stores many redundant boot sectors around the disk (so one damaged sector won't kill the machine), and supports 128 or more partitions versus MBR's 4. The lesson notes MBR, not GPT, is now the legacy standard.

questions.questionHtml: What are the two file locations GRUB loads from on a legacy MBR system versus a UEFI/GPT system, respectively (Stage 1)?

options.html: MBR system: boot.img in the first 440 bytes of the MBR; UEFI/GPT system: grubx64.efi on an EFI partition or in /boot
MBR system: grub.cfg in /boot/grub; UEFI/GPT system: boot.img in the MBR
Both systems load grubx64.efi from the same EFI partition
MBR system: /sbin/init; UEFI/GPT system: /lib/systemd/systemd

questions.explanationHtml: On legacy MBR systems, GRUB Stage 1 is boot.img located in the first 440 bytes of the MBR. On UEFI systems using GPT, GRUB Stage 1 is grubx64.efi located on an EFI partition or in /boot.

questions.questionHtml: Match each GRUB stage (legacy MBR/BIOS path) to what it does or where it lives.
choices: Located in the first 440 bytes of the MBR; loads Grub Stage 1.5
Located between the bootstrap and the first partition in the MBR
Loads the grub menu, then reads /boot/grub/grub.cfg to list available kernels
questions.explanationHtml: GRUB's legacy MBR path has three stages: Stage 1 (boot.img) in the first 440 bytes of the MBR loads Stage 1.5; Stage 1.5 (core.img) sits between the bootstrap and the first partition; Stage 2 (normal.mod) loads the grub menu and reads grub.cfg, which lists the Linux kernels available to load.

questions.questionHtml: In the lesson's grub.cfg excerpt, which command loads the actual Linux Kernel file (e.g., /boot/vmlinuz-4.15.0-76-generic)?

options.html: linux
insmod
search
menuentry

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states: "The kernel is loaded with the command linux. The file /boot/vmlinuz-4.15.0-76-generic contains the Linux Kernel."

questions.questionHtml: Why is the Linux Kernel described as a "Monolithic" kernel in the lesson?

options.html: It exposes all functionality (CPU scheduling, memory management, file management) to the user via system calls, which are how programs request kernel services
It only runs one process at a time
It cannot be extended with modules
It requires a full rebuild to add any new hardware support

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson describes the Linux kernel as monolithic because system calls expose all functionality to the user, such as CPU scheduling, memory management, and file management. A system call is how a program requests services from the kernel; everything on the system occurs through a system call.

questions.questionHtml: What does it mean that the Linux Kernel is "Modular," and what happens if a module fails?

options.html: Modules extend base kernel functionality without requiring a rebuild; if a module fails, that functionality stops but the machine keeps running
Modules replace the entire kernel at runtime; a module failure causes a kernel panic and reboot
Modules are only used for GRUB configuration, not the kernel
Modules cannot be listed or inspected once loaded

questions.explanationHtml: Modules are extensions to base Linux kernel functionality. This modularity allows modification of baseline system functionality without rebuilding the kernel, and module failures will not stop the machine from starting — only the functionality that relies on that module stops.

questions.questionHtml: Once the kernel finishes loading, what program is it hard coded to execute to begin bringing the system to full functionality?

options.html: /sbin/init
/boot/grub/grub.cfg
/etc/environment
/etc/profile

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states: "The kernel, once loaded, is hard coded to reach out and execute /sbin/init. This starts the process of bringing the system to a desired level of functionality using Initialization Daemons."

questions.questionHtml: Match each SysV Run Level to its meaning.
choices: Halt (shutdown the system)
Single user, no network, used for troubleshooting
Multi-user with complete networking and a GUI desktop
Reboot the system
questions.explanationHtml: Per the lesson's Run Level table: 0=Halt/Shutdown, 1=Single User (no network, troubleshooting), 5=Multi-user mode with networking and GUI Desktop, 6=Reboot. (Levels 2/3 are multi-user without/with networking, and 4 is user-definable/not used.)

questions.questionHtml: In SysV init, what does the naming scheme of scripts in /etc/rc#.d (e.g., S01acpid vs. K01atd) indicate?

options.html: The leading letter (S or K) means Start or Kill the process, and the following two-digit number dictates execution order
The leading letter identifies the run level, and the number identifies the daemon's process ID
S means the script is a symbolic link, K means it's a real file
The number identifies which systemd target the script belongs to

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson explains: the first letter K or S means Kill or Start the process that script handles, and the two-digit number that follows dictates the order the scripts execute. These scripts are symbolically linked to scripts in /etc/init.d.

questions.questionHtml: In SysV, what determines the default run level the system tries to reach on boot, and what happens if it fails?

options.html: The initdefault entry in /etc/inittab sets the default; if it fails, the system displays an error and executes the scripts in run level 0 (halt)
The default.target symlink in /lib/systemd/system sets it; if it fails, systemd retries indefinitely
/etc/environment sets it; if it fails, the kernel panics
GRUB's grub.cfg sets it directly with no fallback

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states the system will, by default, try to start the initdefault run level specified in /etc/inittab. If that fails to start, the machine will display an error, then execute the scripts in the 0 (halt) run level.

questions.questionHtml: What is a "daemon" in Linux, as described in the lesson?

options.html: Another name for a background process/service, such as one enabling DHCP or SSH
A synonym for a run level
The first process spawned directly by the kernel
A type of partition table like GPT

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states: "Another name for background processes (or services) in Linux is a daemon. Daemons run in the background and maintain user mode functionality such as DHCP or enabling SSH."

questions.questionHtml: Match each SysV Run Level to its corresponding systemd Target unit.
choices: poweroff.target
rescue.target
multi-user.target
graphical.target
reboot.target
questions.explanationHtml: The lesson's translation table maps SysV run levels to systemd targets: 0→poweroff.target, 1→rescue.target, 2/3/4→multi-user.target, 5→graphical.target, 6→reboot.target.

questions.questionHtml: In systemd, what is /sbin/init symbolically linked to, and what does it interact with?

options.html: /lib/systemd/systemd; it interacts with flat configuration files called units
/etc/init; it interacts with /etc/inittab
/boot/grub/grub.cfg; it interacts with kernel modules
/etc/rc.d; it interacts with shell scripts only

questions.explanationHtml: Systemd starts with the kernel spawning /sbin/init, which is symbolically linked to /lib/systemd/systemd. systemd interacts with flat configuration files called units, with target and service units determining system initialization.

questions.questionHtml: What is the difference between "Wants=" and "Requires=" in a systemd target unit?

options.html: Wants= attempts to start other units but the calling target still executes if they fail; Requires= means the calling target will fail to execute if the dependency fails
Wants= is mandatory and Requires= is optional
Wants= and Requires= are functionally identical
Wants= only applies to service units, Requires= only applies to target units

questions.explanationHtml: Per the lesson: Wants=display-manager.service attempts to start other units, and if they fail to start, the calling target unit still executes. Requires=multi-user.target attempts to start other units, and if they fail, the calling target unit will fail to execute.

questions.questionHtml: Which systemctl command lists the tree of unit dependencies for a given target, such as graphical.target?

options.html: systemctl list-dependencies graphical.target
systemctl cat graphical.target
systemctl list-unit-files
systemctl show -p Wants graphical.target

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson demonstrates systemctl list-dependencies graphical.target to list unit dependencies in tree form. systemctl show -p Wants shows wants to individual units, systemctl cat concatenates a unit file's contents, and systemctl list-unit-files lists every unit file.

questions.questionHtml: According to the lesson, how many locations around the file system do target units search for wants/requires dependencies?

options.html: Eleven
Four
Two
Six

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson notes that wants and requires statements can come from other locations on the file system, and "Target units search for dependencies in eleven other locations around the file system," listing examples like /etc/systemd/system/*, /lib/systemd/system/*, and /run/systemd/generator/*.

questions.questionHtml: What is the last thing to start in the SysV init sequence, and what command specified in inittab displays it?

options.html: A login prompt on each virtual console; the getty command displays it, invoking /bin/login
The GRUB menu; the linux command displays it
The graphical.target; the systemctl command displays it
/etc/environment; the export command displays it

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson states: "The last thing to start is the login program. init spawns a login to each of the Linux virtual consoles. The getty command specified in the inittab displays this login. When given a login name, getty invokes /bin/login, which prompts the user for a password."

questions.questionHtml: Match each Post Boot shell/environment file to its behavior.
choices: Sets Global Variables for every user/process; read once at Init completion, requires a restart to apply changes
Executes for every interactive login shell (system-wide); sets the bash prompt via bash.bashrc and runs *.sh scripts in a .d directory
Executes only for an interactive LOGIN shell, on a per-user basis (e.g., via ssh/telnet)
Executes only for an interactive NON-LOGIN shell, on a per-user basis
questions.explanationHtml: /etc/environment sets Global Variables system-wide and is read once at Init, requiring a restart to apply changes. /etc/profile runs on every interactive login, sourcing /etc/bash.bashrc and any *.sh script in /etc/profile.d. .bash_profile (.profile) runs per-user on interactive login shells (e.g., ssh). .bashrc runs per-user on interactive non-login shells (e.g., spawning a new bash instance without re-authenticating).

questions.questionHtml: Why is /etc/environment not a bash script like other post-boot files?

options.html: It is part of PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules), used to authenticate users in Linux
It is written in Python instead of bash
It is generated dynamically by systemd at every boot
It is a GRUB configuration file, not a shell file

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson notes: "The /etc/environment file is part of PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) used to authenticate users in Linux. That is why it isn't a bash script like everything else."

questions.questionHtml: Why should a cyber operator pay close attention to the Post Boot stage (/etc/environment, /etc/profile, .bash_profile, .bashrc) when assessing a Linux system's security?

options.html: These files are easily changeable, unlike earlier boot stages, and adversaries can abuse that flexibility to run any script they want at login
These files control the BIOS/UEFI Secured Boot setting
These files directly control the MBR boot signature
These files are read before the kernel loads, so they control which kernel modules load

questions.explanationHtml: The lesson warns: "Each locate presented in the post boot process is easily changeable unlike earlier stages of the boot process. Adversaries can take advantage of this flexibility to run any script they want. Be mindful of that when evaluating a Linux system."

title: Windows Process Validity
summary: Windows Process Validity teaches cyber operators how to tell a legitimate Windows process, DLL, service, or scheduled task apart from one that malware is using to hide, persist, or masquerade as something benign. The module walks through the core enumeration commands - PowerShell's Get-Process, Get-Ciminstance, and Get-Service, and cmd.exe's tasklist, sc, schtasks, and netstat - that operators use to inventory what is actually running, which parent process spawned it, what DLLs it loaded, and what network connections it holds. It also covers the registry Run/RunOnce autorun keys and scheduled tasks that malware commonly abuses for persistence, including a hands-on demo that creates a disguised, base64-encoded scheduled task that opens a listening port. Finally it teaches the red flags of an invalid process - misspelled names, wrong install paths, duplicate or unusually high PIDs, and abnormal network ports - skills that matter equally for offensive operators protecting their own toolset and defensive operators hunting intrusions that could put personnel at risk.
