facts: Process validity is the skill of distinguishing a known-good process from a possible bad one based on its attributes and characteristics.
Malware typically hides using stealth and obfuscation in processes, files, registry keys, and drivers, often by mimicking or hooking legitimate processes or services.

In offensive cyber operations, operators must protect their own toolset and check the target box for other malware that could compromise their tools; in defensive operations they must find malware and protect sensitive information, which the lesson notes could be the difference between life and death for soldiers on mission.
The lesson states that processes, services, and daemons are all the same underlying thing.
A DLL cannot execute directly and depends on an executable, such as rundll32.exe, to act as its entry point.
A Windows service is a long-running executable that runs in the background, can be set to auto-start at boot or logon, can be paused and restarted, and does not present a user interface.
PowerShell's Get-Process and cmd.exe's tasklist are the two core built-in commands the lesson identifies for viewing running processes.
Get-Ciminstance Win32_Process exposes the ParentProcessId property, letting an operator see PID-to-PPID relationships that Get-Process does not show.
Windows services can be inspected with Get-Ciminstance Win32_service, Get-Service, sc query, or net start.
Scheduled tasks let a program launch at a pre-set time, at boot, or at logon, and the lesson calls them an easy way to hide malware and establish persistence.
Autorun-related registry locations include the Run and RunOnce keys under HKLM and HKCU, the HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services key, and per-user Run/RunOnce keys under HKU\<SID>.

The lesson's schtasks /Create demo builds a task named "IchBinBosh" that runs a hidden, base64-encoded PowerShell command every 15 minutes to open a listener on port 6666, illustrating how attackers disguise malicious command lines; the demo's own output shows it running under the operator's own (non-admin) logon, not an elevated account.
Base64-encoded PowerShell commands run via the -encode/-encodedCommand switch can be decoded using a tool such as CyberChef.
netstat's -a, -n, -o, and -b switches respectively show all connections/listening ports, numeric addresses, the owning PID, and the executable tied to each connection, with -b requiring admin rights.

Legitimate Windows system processes typically run from C:\Windows\System32, while third-party software such as Chrome runs from elsewhere (e.g., C:\Program Files), so an unexpected path is a red flag.

Warning signs of a suspicious process include misspelled names (such as "scvhost" instead of "svchost"), non-standard listening ports, multiple instances of a process that should be unique (such as LSASS or SMSS), and a system process running with an unusually high PID.
In the lesson's "Where's Waldo" task-list exercise, the giveaways were a second smss.exe running with an abnormally high PID, plus the unfamiliar/misspelled processes bad.exe and reqedit.exe.

GUI alternatives to the command-line tools include Task Manager and Process Explorer for processes, services.msc and PsService for services, Task Scheduler and Autoruns for scheduled tasks/persistence, and TCPView for network connections.

questions.questionHtml: According to the lesson, what is a DLL (Dynamic Link Library)?

options.html: A non-standalone program that can be linked to and run by multiple programs at the same time, and cannot be directly executed on its own.
A standalone executable that runs independently in its own Windows session.
A registry key used to store scheduled task triggers.
A background service that always displays a user interface.

questions.explanationHtml: A DLL is a non-standalone program that can be run by (linked to) multiple programs at the same time. It cannot be directly executed — it's dependent on an exe to use as an entry point, such as RUNDLL.EXE, which calls on the functionality of the DLL.

questions.questionHtml: Which statement about a Windows Service is correct, according to the lesson?

options.html: It's a long-running executable that runs in its own Windows session in the background, can be set to auto-start at boot or logon, and can be paused and restarted.
It always displays a user interface while running.
It must be launched manually by the user every time the computer boots.
It is simply a DLL that has been compiled into an executable.

questions.explanationHtml: Services are long-running executables that run in their own Windows sessions (in the background). They can be set to auto start when the computer boots or a user logs on, can be paused and restarted, and do not interact with/show any user interface.
